title: Why Do Humans Tell Stories?
paragraphs: Storytelling has every claim to be a human universal; ethnographers have yet to document a society entirely without it. From cosmological myth and folk tale to the novel, the feature film and the video game, narrative remains among the foremost means by which human beings render experience intelligible, transmit norms and divert one another.

For the overwhelming majority of our history, narratives were transmitted orally. Before the invention of writing, communities entrusted storytellers with the custody of collective memory, the explanation of natural phenomena and the modelling of conduct. Metre, repetition and formulaic diction were thus less ornament than mnemonic architecture, enabling lengthy compositions to endure across generations.

The emergence of writing allowed some of these traditions to be fixed on clay and parchment. The Epic of Gilgamesh, from ancient Mesopotamia, is commonly counted among the earliest extant works of literature, and its meditation on friendship, mortality and the hubris of seeking to transcend them retains a disconcerting contemporaneity.

Accounts of narrative’s enduring hold on us are various. Because stories bind events into chains of cause and affect, the information they encode tends to be retained more readily than discrete facts. They also oblige the reader to inhabit perspectives other than their own, and a body of research has associated fiction reading with heightened social cognition, although both the magnitude and the direction of that association remain contested.
